notes.text: Thou shalt take — This seems to be required of each master of a family, either upon his first settlement, or once every year at one of their three feasts, when they were obliged to go up to Jerusalem.

A Syrian — So Jacob was, partly by his original, as being born of Syrian parents, as were Abraham and Rebecca, both of Chaldea or Mesopotamia, which was a part of Syria largely so called, partly by his education and conversation; and partly by his relations, his wives being such, and his children too by their mother's. Ready to perish - Either through want and poverty; (See Gen. xxviii, 11, 20; xxxii, 10,) or through the rage of his brother Esau, and the treachery of his father-in-law Laban.
It — The basket of first-fruits, ver. 2.

Thou shalt rejoice — Thou shalt hereby enabled to take comfort in all thy employments, when thou hast sanctified them by giving God his portion. It is the will of God, that we should be chearful not only in our attendance upon his holy ordinances, but in our enjoyment of the gifts of his providence. Whatever good thing God gives us, we should make the most comfortable use of it we can, still tracing the streams to the fountain of all consolation.

glossa.text: *And when thou shalt have entered,* etc. Just as the Israelites in the land of promise are bidden to offer their first-fruits for a giving of thanks, because they were snatched out of Egypt, so let us, entering through the spiritual Jordan — that is, baptism — into the land of the Church, place in the basket of our manner of life the first-fruits of good working, and let us offer them to God upon the altar of the catholic faith, that our priest Christ may receive them; and there let us confess to the Lord, saying that the Syrian — who is interpreted "lofty," or "moistening," that is, the devil — was pursuing our father, that is, the first-formed man, that, having deceived him through pride, gluttony and avarice, he might deprive him of the possession of paradise; whence as an exile he sojourned in the Egypt of this world in a small number, because many followed idolatry, and few remained faithful. But after the law was given and more arose, receiving the knowledge and the faith of the one God, the Egyptians — that is, the demons — afflicted them, laying upon them the most grievous burdens of sins. But God looked upon the affliction and the labour of the human race, and sent his Son, who is called his hand and his arm, that he might snatch them out of the power of darkness and carry them over into the kingdom of light. So he handed over to us a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, the mighty Church, where there is the milk of innocence and the honeycomb of doctrine, whereby little ones are nourished, and the honey of a sweet and manifold wisdom, whereby the perfect are filled.

*Which the Lord thy God hath given,* etc. As if to say, I offer nothing but what he has given; for every good thing is from God.

*Of the Lord thy God.* Who will keep them as it were beneath his eyes, and will render them on that day, a just judge.

*Thou shalt feast,* with a spiritual banquet, of which it is said: *Eat, O friends, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved ((Cantic. V))*.

*And the Levite,* the true minister of God, taken from among men and appointed for men in the things that pertain to God.

*A psalm in confession.* Confession is twofold; one is of praise, the other of sins. The confession of praise befits the perfect, the confession of sins those who are beginning *inicipientibus*; whence in this psalm the prophet admonishes to confession. ((CASS.)) This psalm teaches both to praise God unceasingly, and unceasingly to bewail our sins: because neither in evils is one to despair, nor in good things ought the mind to be lifted up. First he enjoins upon the perfect the chief kind of confession, that is, praise.

*Rejoice ye.* ((AUG.)) If the voice rejoices outwardly, etc., *as far as* and in what order and how wonderfully he made it. *All the earth.* Admonishing to praise. Not one corner of the earth does he exhort: but as he knows the blessing to have been sown everywhere, so from everywhere he requires jubilation. *Serve ye in gladness.* ((AUG.)) This servitude is not of bitterness, nor of indignation, but of happiness and of liberty. Let charity therefore make thee a servant, because truth has made thee free. Whence the Lord: *If you shall abide in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed: and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free ((Joan. VIII))*. 

*In gladness.* Because they are set free; not murmuring, as in the desert: whence he subjoins the reward.

*Enter ye into his sight.* It is a great thing to rejoice in the sight of so great a one. *Enter ye in.* ((CASS.)) Secondly, to those about to enter, the second kind of confession; nor let it be doubted, because mercy is with him.

notes.text: Let your gentleness — Yieldingness, sweetness of temper, the result of joy in the Lord. Be known - By your whole behaviour. To all men - Good and bad, gentle and froward. Those of the roughest tempers are good natured to some, from natural sympathy and various motives; a Christian, to all. The Lord - The judge, the rewarder, the avenger. Is at hand - Standeth at the door.

Be anxiously careful for nothing — If men are not gentle towards you, yet neither on this, nor any other account, be careful, but pray. Carefulness and prayer cannot stand together. In every thing - Great and small. Let your requests be made known - They who by a preposterous shame or distrustful modesty, cover, stifle, or keep in their desires, as if they were either too small or too great, must be racked with care; from which they are entirely delivered, who pour them out with a free and filial confidence. To God - It is not always proper to disclose them to men. By supplication - Which is the enlarging upon and pressing our petition. With thanksgiving - The surest mark of a soul free from care, and of prayer joined with true resignation. This is always followed by peace. Peace and thanksgiving are both coupled together, Colossians iii, 15.

And the peace of God — That calm, heavenly repose, that tranquility of spirit, which God only can give. Which surpasseth all understanding - Which none can comprehend, save he that receiveth it. Shall keep - Shall guard, as a garrison does a city. Your hearts - Your affections. Your minds - Your understandings, and all the various workings of them; through the Spirit and power of Christ Jesus, in the knowledge and love of God. Without a guard set on these likewise, the purity and vigour of our affections cannot long be preserved.

Finally — To sum up all. Whatsoever things are true - Here are eight particulars placed in two fourfold rows; the former containing their duty; the latter, the commendation of it. The first word in the former row answers the first in the latter; the second word, the second and so on. True - In speech. Honest - In action. Just - With regard to others. Pure - With regard to yourselves. Lovely - And what more lovely than truth? Of good report - As is honesty, even where it is not practiced. If there be any virtue - And all virtues are contained in justice. If there be any praise - In those things which relate rather to ourselves than to our neighbour. Think on these things - That ye may both practice them yourselves, and recommend them to others.

The things which ye have learned — As catechumens. And received - By continual instructions. And heard and seen - In my life and conversation. These do, and the God of peace shall be with you - Not only the peace of God, but God himself, the fountain of peace.

glossa.text: *Rejoice,* etc. Being gladdened over their faith and their works, the Apostle, that they may be the more eager, desires that they, advancing in this zeal, should rejoice in the Lord, and he repeats it, that he may show that he truly rejoices in them.

*Moderation.* That is, right measure, so that all joy may be in the Lord, and that others may learn this through you. Or, *let moderation be known to all,* faithful and unbelieving, that they may imitate it, lest they be able to reprehend. *The Lord is nigh,* that is, ready to give whatsoever is needful in spiritual or in temporal things. Be solicitous and fearful about nothing. But your petitions concerning those things which you wish to obtain.

*But in every prayer.* Prayer and supplication are made in common for oneself or for others, concerning whatsoever things, but petition is made concerning things necessary by name. *Let them be made known.* This making known comes about by assiduity, and by watchfulness of prayer. Then at last peace keeps the hearts in Christ. He says this for this reason, because he who has peace with God does not fear an adverse mind. *With God.* Or to the angels, who offer them to God. Whence: When you were praying, I offered your prayer before God. Or, let them be made known for us with God through endurance, not with men through boasting.

*And the peace of God,* that is, God, who is the highest peace, which cannot even be thought, and therefore outside him there is need of nothing. *It surpasseth all understanding.* Ours, not that of those who always behold the face of the Father. Or, the peace whereby God himself is at peace *surmounts all understanding:* except his own, because neither can we know it thus, nor can any angels.

*For the rest, brethren,* etc. Thus far he has admonished against persecutors and against false preachers. But for the rest, in the conclusion, he sets forth the things which belong to perfection. *Whatsoever things are just.* This toward one's neighbour. *Holy,* in one's own life; and, that a lesser thing be named, *whatsoever things are lovely,* that is, worthy to be loved, as a modest gait, humble speech and the like.

*Of good report. ((AUG.))* For ourselves our own life, for others a good report is necessary. Accordingly whosoever guards his life from the crimes of shameful deeds does well to himself; but whosoever [guards] his good report is merciful toward others also.

notes.text: Our Lord does not satisfy their curiosity, but corrects the wrong motive they had in seeking him: because ye did eat — Merely for temporal advantage. Hitherto Christ had been gathering hearers: he now begins to try their sincerity, by a figurative discourse concerning his passion, and the fruit of it, to be received by faith.

labour not for the meat which perisheth — For bodily food: not for that only not chiefly: not at all, but in subordination to grace, faith, love, the meat which endureth to everlasting life. labour, work for this; foreverlasting life. So our Lord expressly commands, work for life, as well as from life: from a principle of faith and love. Him hath the Father sealed - By this very miracle, as well as by his whole testimony concerning him. See chap. iii, 33. Sealing is a mark of the authenticity of a writing.
The works of God — Works pleasing to God.
This is the work of God — The work most pleasing to God, and the foundation of all others: that ye believe - He expresses it first properly, afterward figuratively.
What sign dost thou? — Amazing, after what they had just seen!

Our fathers ate manna — This sign Moses gave them. He gave them bread from heaven - From the lower sublunary heaven; to which Jesus opposes the highest heaven: in which sense he says seven times, ver. 32, 33, 38, 50, 58, 62, that he himself came down from heaven.
Moses gave you not bread from heaven — It was not Moses who gave the manna to your fathers; but my Father who now giveth the true bread from heaven. Psalm lxxviii, 24.

He that — giveth life to the world - Not (like the manna) to one people only: and that from generation to generation. Our Lord does not yet say, I am that bread; else the Jews would not have given him so respectful an answer, ver. 34.
Give us this bread — Meaning it still, in a literal sense: yet they seem now to be not far from believing.
I am the bread of life — Having and giving life: he that cometh -he that believeth - Equivalent expressions: shall never hunger, thirst - Shall be satisfied, happy, forever.

glossa.text: *And when they had found him.* Behold, he is present to those from whom he had fled, lest they should make him king. Why then had he fled, if not for the aforesaid sacrament? Again, being present, he speaks to them, that of those whose bellies he filled, he may fill the minds also, saying: *Amen, amen I say to you,* teaching those whom he appointed teachers to flee praise and earthly rule, but nevertheless to press on in preaching.

*Amen, amen I say to you.* After he had treated of his divinity, by which he is the same with the Father and to be honoured with the same honour, and of his humanity, by which he frees from death and raises up, being worthy of great honour, he wishes to treat of the food of life, that is, of the Word of God. And this is the connection as regards the sense. But according to the letter, thus: You seek me, not for my own sake, but for the sake of the loaves that perish. Therefore work, that is, seek me for my own sake, not for the sake of anything else. For he himself is that food which endures unto life everlasting, as he will afterwards say openly. In like manner many seek Jesus daily, not for Jesus' sake, but that it may be well with them in this time.

*God hath sealed.* As by a proper sign he marked him off from the rest, because he who is the Son of man is also the Son of God; and therefore do not despise me, the Son of man, but ask of me spiritual food.

*This is the work of God.* Faith working by love is the work, because if the means be wanting, nothing is required but the will. Deservedly also is that faith called a work which works by love, which is the beginning and the end of all good.

*He said therefore.* Because they preferred the work of Moses to his work, he shows that that was the less, since it was not bread from heaven but only a figure of it, and that his own is the greater, which is the bread from heaven that gives life; and this is the food which he said above endures unto life everlasting.

*For the true bread.* The angels eat the pure Word, solid food; but we the Word, yet turned into milk, because if we cannot eat, we can suck. For unless he were made flesh, he would not be known by us, he would not be tasted by us.

*Lord, always,* etc. As the Samaritan woman, hearing: *He that shall drink of this water shall not thirst for ever,* took it according to the body, and yet, wishing to be without labour and want, said: *Give me this water,* so these seek a bread which may refresh them and never fail, on account of which they wished to make him king. But Jesus calls them back to himself, and more evidently opens what bread he spoke of: *I am the bread of life.* I shall be able to give life, because I am the bread that gives life, baked and formed by the fire of the Holy Spirit in the oven of the virginal womb, and given to the world to drive away the hunger of the ignorance of God.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.
echoes.note: 'The Lord is at hand' (ho kyrios engys) most closely matches 'The LORD is near to all who call on him' (engys kyrios), grounding Paul's nearness claim and its link to prayer in v.6. High lexical volume on engys, coherence with the prayer/petition context, and availability in the LXX Psalter make this the strongest source for the phrase.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, and rejoice, you righteous! Shout for joy, all you who are upright in heart!
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD always' echoes the recurrent Psalter imperative 'Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, you righteous' (32:11; cf. 33:1; 97:12). Recurrence is strong across the Psalter and coherence with Paul's joy theme is high; volume is moderate because Paul universalizes 'always' beyond any single psalm.

echoes.text: Be glad in Yahweh, you righteous people! Give thanks to his holy Name.
echoes.note: 'Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous' supplies the same divine-object joy imperative that Paul doubles for emphasis. The Psalter's habitual call to rejoice in the LORD is available and coherent, though the volume of any single verse is moderate given the formula's diffusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted' reinforces the 'Lord is near' motif with the same engys idiom, and Psalm 34 broadly underwrites Paul's confidence in deliverance. Recurrence of the nearness formula with Psalm 145 strengthens coherence, though volume per verse is moderate.

echoes.text: Be silent at the presence of the Lord Yahweh, for the day of Yahweh is at hand. For Yahweh has prepared a sacrifice. He has consecrated his guests.
echoes.note: 'The day of the LORD is at hand/near' supplies the eschatological-imminence sense of 'The Lord is at hand,' if Paul means the Lord's coming rather than his presence. Availability in the prophetic day-of-the-Lord tradition and coherence with Philippians' Parousia hope (3:20) support this, though it competes with the Psalter nearness reading.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you' parallels Paul's 'peace of God which surpasses all understanding will guard your hearts,' linking divine peace, the mind, and protective keeping. Coherence is strong on the guarding-peace-of-the-mind motif; volume is moderate because Paul does not quote the phrasing verbatim.

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' parallels Paul's remedy for anxiety: hand your requests to God in prayer rather than carry them. Coherence with the anti-anxiety-through-petition logic is strong; volume is moderate since Paul shares the idea, not the wording.

echoes.text: In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep, for you, Yahweh alone, make me live in safety.
echoes.note: 'In peace I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety' offers the OT pairing of divine peace with security from anxiety that underlies 'do not be anxious... and the peace of God will guard you.' Volume is low and the link thematic, so this is a contributing echo.

echoes.text: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
echoes.note: 'Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad' supplies a wisdom backdrop for Paul's 'in nothing be anxious.' Volume and verbal overlap are slight, but the heart-anxiety theme is available in the sapiential tradition, making this a faint echo.

echoes.text: And if a man loves righteousness, The fruits of wisdom’s labor are virtues, For she teaches soberness and understanding, righteousness and courage; And there is nothing in life for men more profitable than these.
echoes.note: Wisdom's praise of the cardinal virtues ('she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage') models the Hellenistic-Jewish virtue list Paul adapts, especially the terms for 'just' and the framing of virtue (arete) itself, which Paul uses uniquely here. Coherence with the Wisdom tradition's moral catalogues makes this a plausible deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.
echoes.note: Paul's virtue catalogue (true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report) draws on the sapiential ideal of the pure heart and gracious speech that wins favor. Recurrence of these virtue terms in Proverbs and the wider Hellenistic-Jewish moral tradition supplies availability, but the volume of any one verse is low.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'So you will find favor and good repute (LXX: good things) in the sight of God and man' parallels Paul's 'whatever is of good report' and the appeal to public commendation. Volume is low and the link conceptual, but the good-repute motif is available in the sapiential tradition.

echoes.text: You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.
echoes.note: 'The God of peace will be with you' continues the divine-peace motif of v.7 and resonates with Isaiah's promise that God keeps in peace those whose minds are fixed on him. Volume is faint here and the title 'God of peace' is Paul's own, so this is a low-grade continuation echo of the peace tradition.

echoes.text: Then Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh, and called it “Yahweh is Peace.” To this day it is still in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
echoes.note: Gideon's altar 'The LORD is peace' (YHWH-shalom) offers an OT antecedent for naming God by his peace, loosely behind Paul's 'the God of peace.' The volume is very low and the connection figural, but it documents the availability of associating God's name with shalom.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He rained down manna on them to eat, and gave them food from the sky.
echoes.note: 'He gave them bread out of heaven to eat' (v.31) is a formal citation ('as it is written') closest in wording to LXX Psalm 78:24 ('arton ouranou edoken autois'). The chapter's hermeneutical hinge; maximal Volume.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: 'I am about to rain bread from heaven for you' is the originating text behind the v.31 citation; Jesus directly contests its meaning ('it was not Moses who gave...'). The quotation conflates Exodus 16 with Psalm 78, so both are primary sources.

echoes.text: and gave them bread from the sky for their hunger, and brought water out of the rock for them for their thirst, and commanded them that they should go in to possess the land which you had sworn to give them.
echoes.note: 'You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger' is a third witness to the formula the crowd cites, showing the manna-from-heaven line was a fixed liturgical commonplace (Recurrence) rather than a single text.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? and your labor for that which doesn’t satisfy? listen diligently to me, and eat you that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. Turn your ear, and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live: and I will make an everlasting covenant with […]
echoes.note: 'Why spend money for that which is not bread... eat what is good... that your soul may live' undergirds Jesus' contrast between 'food which perishes' and 'food which remains to eternal life' (v.27). Coherent invitation-to-true-nourishment background.

echoes.text: Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.” Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and became foul: and Moses was angry with them. They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
echoes.note: The manna that bred worms and stank when hoarded overnight gives concrete force to 'the food which perishes' (v.27). A plausible but faint verbal-conceptual link within the active manna matrix; contested as deliberate.

echoes.text: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
echoes.note: Wisdom's invitation 'Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' stands behind 'I am the bread of life. He who comes to me will not hunger.' Strong Coherence: Jesus speaks as personified Wisdom hosting a banquet that confers life.

echoes.text: Come to me, you that are desirous of me, And be you filled with my produce. For my memorial is sweeter than honey, And my inheritance than the honeycomb. They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more, those who drink me will thirst for more.' John inverts it ('will never hunger... never thirst'), a deliberate transformation signalling Jesus surpasses Wisdom/Torah. High Availability and Coherence; the inversion is the point.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: 'They shall not hunger or thirst... he who has pity will lead them' supplies the hunger-and-thirst-abolished promise of the eschatological return. Coheres tightly with v.35's double negation; an exilic-restoration backdrop to the bread of life.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The repeated 'I will raise him up at the last day' (vv.39-40) draws on the clearest OT resurrection text, 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake... to everlasting life.' Provides the Availability for John's last-day raising; recurs across the discourse.
